     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"
     23	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145	
     146	## References
     147	
     148	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     149	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     150	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     151	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     152	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     153	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     154	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     155	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     156	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     157	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     158	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "7d13192a-31ad-4a07-975a-6c064c7f56df", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_mHCB8aithVkbYeK13WVhbZ", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history (when it first entered ALARM).
     17	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     18	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     19	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     20	
     21	### Step 2: Build the context
     22	
     23	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     24	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     25	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     26	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     27	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.
     28	
     29	### Step 2b: Rule EBS in or out (chat requests with no EBS alarm only)
     30	
     31	This check runs only when the run did not start from an AWS/EBS alarm or an `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` alarm, for example a chat request such as "my app is slow, is it storage?". When an EBS alarm triggered the run, skip this step and run Steps 3 to 6 in full.
     32	
     33	Read `CPUUtilization` for the instance, and the latency, `VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance` (gp2, st1, sc1) and instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` (if published) for the volumes found in Step 2, over the same window. Use the qualitative attribution matrix in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). Report "Not EBS" and stop tuning storage only if all of these hold: CPU is high, volume latency and queue length are normal, no `DescribeVolumeStatus` problem was found, and no burst or instance balance is draining or at 0. Otherwise continue with Step 3.
     34	
     35	### Step 3: Measure each volume on the dimension(s) its type is limited by
     36	
     37	Pull the last 30 minutes of AWS/EBS metrics at 1-minute granularity.
     38	
     39	- Actual IOPS = (VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds
     40	- Actual throughput = (VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period, in MiB/s
     41	- Avg latency in ms per operation = Sum(VolumeTotalReadTime) / Sum(VolumeReadOps) x 1,000, and the same for writes with VolumeTotalWriteTime and VolumeWriteOps. VolumeTotalReadTime and VolumeTotalWriteTime are in seconds, so the x 1,000 converts to milliseconds. `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` are already in milliseconds
     42	- VolumeQueueLength
     43	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both dimensions, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 for MiB/s. `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only. If `VolumeAvg*` returns nothing, use the Sum-based math above.
     44	- Always read `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds in the period with no read or write submitted; `VolumeId` only). Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period seconds x 100. Report it as evidence for every volume. Near 0 means I/O was submitted for the whole period, which fits both saturation and impairment, so use Step 5 to tell them apart. A volume that is mostly idle during the alarm window is unlikely to be the binding volume. There is no fixed band; compare with the volume's own history.
     45	
     46	Apply the rule for the volume's type:
     47	
     48	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     49	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     50	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops AND actual MiB/s to the volume's throughput limit; either can bind. Throughput is not provisioned separately, but the documented throughput limit depends on the provisioned IOPS (see the io1 and io2 rows in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md)). Compute the limit from `Iops` with those rules, then compare. Do NOT use VolumeThroughputPercentage to judge throughput on io1/io2; it reports the % of provisioned IOPS delivered.
     51	- st1/sc1: throughput-oriented with burst credits; compare MiB/s to the baseline/burst for the size and check BurstBalance.
     52	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     53	
     54	### Step 4: Check the instance layer
     55	
     56	- Sum actual IOPS and MiB/s across all attached volumes; compare to the instance type's EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes.
     57	- Aggregate across ALL attached volumes, including the root volume.
     58	- Check EBSIOBalance% / EBSByteBalance%. If they are draining or at 0, or the sum is at the instance limit, the INSTANCE is the binding layer and raising volume provisioning will not help.
     59	- If instance metrics are healthy and a volume is at its own limit, the VOLUME is the binding layer.
     60	- If `EBSIOBalance%` is absent, the instance size does not publish it. Use the summed values against the baseline.

     63	
     64	If queue length and latency are elevated but the volume and instance are both below their limits, this is NOT saturation. Suspect an impairment or injected latency; do NOT recommend increasing provisioning.

     66	The impairment signature is IOPS and throughput collapsing while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Saturation looks different: metrics flat at the provisioned limit with modest latency. When you see the impairment signature, check in this order:

     94	## Other performance topics
     95	
     96	### Micro-bursting
     97	
     98	AWS/EBS data is 1-minute. Sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average stays below it. If latency or queue length rises while the average is below the limit, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. Do not claim headroom from the average alone.

     101	
     102	A volume created from a snapshot loads blocks from Amazon S3 the first time they are read, which adds latency until the volume is initialized.      106	- Volume level: gp2, st1 and sc1 publish `BurstBalance`. Draining or at 0 means the volume has dropped or will drop to its baseline. Recommend gp2 to gp3 migration, or a size or type that gives the needed baseline.

     110	
     111	1. Measure peak demand per volume over a representative window (IOPS and MiB/s, Step 3 math).
     112	2.      3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.

     19	
     20	- `VolumeThroughputPercentage` exists only for Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes. It reports the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered, not MiB/s. Never use it as a throughput signal on io1 or io2. A healthy io2 volume can read 100% while its MiB/s is low.
     21	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. For io1 and io2, compute the throughput limit from the provisioned IOPS with the rules in the table.
     22	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both the `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` dimensions and exist only for Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 to get MiB/s.
     23	- `VolumeStalledIOCheck` also uses the `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` dimensions and exists only for Nitro instances.
     24	- `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only.
     25	- `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds. Average latency in ms per operation = Sum(time) / Sum(ops) x 1,000.
     26	- A 1-minute average hides sub-minute peaks. If the minute average is below a limit but latency and queue length rise, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven.
     27	
     28	## Latency expectations (documented only)
     29	
     30	| Type | Documented expectation |
     31	|---|---|
     32	| gp3 | Single-digit millisecond latency |
     33	| io2 Block Express | Under 500 microseconds average latency for 16 KiB I/O |
     34	
     35	For other types the public documentation does not give a latency number. Compare the volume against its own history in the same window on a normal day and against the type's documented expectation above.
     36	
     37	## Not encoded on purpose
     38	
     39	The drafts carried latency bands (for example "io2 below 1 ms, gp3 below 2 ms, st1 below 10 ms"), a queue length rule ("1 per 1,000 provisioned IOPS"), `VolumeIdleTime` bands, `BurstBalance` bands and percentage triggers ("below 95%", "above 90% of provisioned"). No public AWS source states these, so they are not in this skill.
     40	
     41	## Saturation and impairment signatures
     42	
     43	| Signature | What you see | What it means | What to recommend |
     44	|---|---|---|---|
     45	| Volume saturation | IOPS or MiB/s flat at the volume's provisioned limit. Latency modest. Instance layer healthy | The volume is the binding layer | Raise the bound dimension, sized within the instance's EBS baseline |
     46	| Instance saturation | Sum across all attached volumes flat at the instance EBS baseline, or `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` draining or at 0. Each volume below its own limit | The instance is the binding layer | Change the instance type. Raising volume provisioning will not help |
     47	| Burst credits exhausted | gp2, st1 or sc1 `BurstBalance` at or near 0, throughput or IOPS dropped to baseline | Burst credits are the binding layer | gp2 to gp3 migration, or a type or size change that gives the needed baseline |
     48	| Impairment or injected latency | IOPS and throughput collapse while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Volume and instance below their limits | Not saturation. An AWS-side impairment, a fault injection, or a non-EBS cause. The pattern alone does not prove which | Never recommend more provisioning. Check volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health and AWS FIS (see troubleshoot-performance.md Step 5). Name AWS-side impairment only with a direct signal; otherwise the cause stays Indeterminate |
     49	
     50	## Sources
     51	
     52	- gp3 and gp2: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/general-purpose.html
     53	- io1 and io2 (IOPS and throughput limits): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/provisioned-iops.html
     54	- Volume type comparison: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/ebs-volume-types.html
     55	- st1 and sc1: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/hdd-vols.html
     56	- Amazon CloudWatch metrics for Amazon EBS (units, dimensions, `VolumeThroughputPercentage`): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/using_cloudwatch_ebs.html

## Root cause
The rise in write latency and VolumeQueueLength on gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 (attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_2) comes from a planned fault-injection test. The volume is not running out of capacity. AWS FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (template EXT1234567890abcdef_4, role example-fis, tag Project=example) is running the aws:ebs:volume-io-latency action against this one volume. Its parameters are 500 ms latency on 100% of writes and 50% of reads, for PT60M. The action started at 16:47:16Z. The experiment has no stop condition, so it will keep running until about 17:47Z unless someone stops it. The workload is steady at about 500 write IOPS against 3,000 provisioned, and there is no sign the IOPS or throughput limit was hit. Adding IOPS would not help, because the latency is injected artificially and is not caused by saturation. Next step: confirm with the experiment owner. If the impact is not acceptable, stop the experiment with FIS StopExperiment on EXP1234567890abcdef_7. Latency should return to about 0.95 ms once it ends.

- CloudWatch VolumeWriteOps: about 30,000 per minute (about 500 IOPS) throughout; the 16:47Z drop to 25,872 shows writes stalling, not more demand
- ec2:DescribeVolumes: gp3 with 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s provisioned; the workload uses about 17% of the IOPS
- VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck returned no data points in the 16:20–16:49Z window, so no performance limit was hit
- Earlier experiments from the same template (EXP1234567890abcdef_4 at 16:15Z, EXP1234567890abcdef_8 at 08:35Z) were stopped by a user, which fits a repeated test pattern

", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "**No, don't add IOPS.** The volume isn't running out of capacity. A running AWS FIS fault-injection experiment is adding 500 ms of delay to its I/O.

**Root cause:** FIS experiment `EXP1234567890abcdef_7` (template `EXT1234567890abcdef_4`, tag `Project=example`) targets only `vol-0123456789abcdef0`.
- **Who started it:** CloudTrail shows `StartExperiment` at 16:47:04Z by `assumed-role/Admin/example-session`, from aws-cli.
- **What it does:** the action is `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency`. It adds 500 ms to 100% of writes and 50% of reads.
- **How long:** the action started at 16:47:16Z and runs for 60 minutes. It will end on its own at about 17:47Z.
- **No safety net:** the experiment has no stop condition.

**What the volume metrics show (1-minute data):**

| Metric | 16:21–16:46Z (before) | 16:48Z (during) |
|---|---|---|
| IOPS | ~1,000 (500 read + 500 write) | 41.9 |
| Throughput | 15.6 MiB/s | 0.65 MiB/s |
| Average write latency | 0.953 ms | 503.6 ms |
| `VolumeQueueLength` | ~0.77 | 16.0 |
| Idle time | ~52% | 0.46 s per minute |

The change started in the same minute as the experiment (16:47Z). The application keeps about 16 I/Os outstanding, and each one now waits around 500 ms. So IOPS drops as latency rises, which is the pattern of injected latency, not a full volume.

**Why more IOPS won't help:**
- **Volume:** it's provisioned for 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s. Before the test it used about 33% of its IOPS and 12.5% of its throughput.
- **Instance:** `i-1234567890abcdef0_2` (c6i.large) is also well under its limits. Burst credit balances (`EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`) were 99%, CPU about 1.4%, and demand was below its EBS baseline of 3,600 IOPS and ~77.5 MiB/s.
- **Not an AWS-side fault:** the stalled-I/O check (`VolumeStalledIOCheck`) reads 0 and the volume status checks pass. There are no open AWS Health events for EBS or EC2 in us-east-1.

**What to do:**
- Confirm with the experiment owner (dewavic, project `example`) that this test is intended.
- If the impact isn't acceptable, stop the experiment (FIS `StopExperiment` on `EXP1234567890abcdef_7`). Write latency should drop back to about 0.95 ms.
- Otherwise it clears by itself at about 17:47Z.
- For future runs, give template `EXT1234567890abcdef_4` a stop condition tied to a CloudWatch alarm (this queue-length alarm or an application latency alarm).
- I've started a separate mitigation plan along these lines; it will appear as its own report.

**Other things I noticed (they don't change the answer):**
- **Alarm state:** when I checked at about 16:49Z, alarm `example-d-gp3-queue-length` still read OK (last change 08:47:48Z). It needs 3 minutes in a row above 4 and the first such minute was 16:48Z, so it should switch to ALARM around 16:50–16:51Z.
- **Earlier alarms:** it went into ALARM at 07:43Z and 08:39Z today and twice on 11 Nov. Those three times today line up with earlier runs of the same template, and today's runs before this one were stopped by a user. It has no alarm actions configured.
- **Instance ceiling:** the three attached volumes are provisioned for a combined 12,000 IOPS and 500 MiB/s, well above the c6i.large baseline of 3,600 IOPS and ~77.5 MiB/s. If this volume ever does need more IOPS, the instance would limit it first.

**What I couldn't check:**
- Only about two minutes of data existed after the latency started.
- I didn't look at application-level metrics or logs, so the app impact is inferred from EBS metrics.
- My check of recent volume modifications returned an error for this volume, so the other two volumes went unchecked. I didn't search CloudTrail for volume changes either.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

## Results
## Mitigation proposal: injected EBS I/O latency on vol-0123456789abcdef0

**Should you add IOPS? No.** Leave the volume at 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s, with no ModifyVolume. The volume is not out of capacity. An AWS FIS experiment is adding 500 ms of latency to its I/O, and more provisioned IOPS or throughput would not change that.

**Do you need to act now? Only if the owner says so.** You have two options:
- **Stop it now:** stop FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7, but only if the owner (dewavic, Project=example) confirms the impact is unintended or unacceptable.
- **Let it run:** it ends on its own at about 17:47Z. It is 16:50Z now, so about 57 minutes of injection remain.

Whichever you choose, add an alarm-based stop condition to template EXT1234567890abcdef_4 so that later runs stop themselves.

### Current state I read (account 012345678901_1, us-east-1)
- **Experiment** `[redacted ARN]`:
  - Status is `running`.
  - Action `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` started at 16:47:16Z, with duration PT60M.
  - It injects write latency of 500 ms into 100% of writes and read latency of 500 ms into 50% of reads.
  - The only target is `vol-0123456789abcdef0`.
  - Stop conditions: `source: none`.
- **Template** `EXT1234567890abcdef_4` (Name `example-d-latency`): it also has `stopConditions: [{source: none}]`. It was last updated at 16:47:01Z, 3 seconds before this run started, which fits a scripted, deliberate test.
- **Alarm** `example-d-gp3-queue-length`: it has no actions. When I read it at 16:50Z it still showed `OK`, last changed at 08:47:48Z. It needs 3 of 3 one-minute datapoints above 4, and metrics arrive with a delay, so it may not have switched to ALARM yet.

### Plan
I checked this plan against the safe-deployment policies. One "delete/terminate denied" violation remains open, and I judged it a false positive. FIS StopExperiment deletes no resource or data. It only ends the fault injection, which takes the volume back to its pre-experiment state. You can re-run the test from the template whenever you want.

**Prepare**
1. Save the template configuration as your rollback baseline:
   `aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --region us-east-1 > fis-template-EXT1234567890abcdef_4-before.json`
2. Save the experiment configuration so you can repeat the test exactly:
   `aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 > fis-experiment-EXP1234567890abcdef_7.json`

**Check before acting**
3. Confirm the experiment is still running and only targets `vol-0123456789abcdef0`:
   `aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 --query 'experiment.{status:state.status,targets:targets.Volumes.resourceArns}'`
   - If the status is `completed` or `stopped`, skip step 4.
4. Get explicit confirmation from dewavic (Project=example) that the impact is unintended or unacceptable. If this is a planned test, do not stop it; let it finish at about 17:47Z.

**Apply**
5. Stop the injection (only after step 4 confirms):
   `aws fis stop-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1`
   - A stopped experiment cannot be resumed. To repeat the test you have to start a new run.
6. Add a stop condition so later runs halt on their own. This does not affect the run that is already going.
   `aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --region us-east-1 --stop-conditions source=aws:cloudwatch:alarm,value=[redacted ARN]`
   - Instead, you can point it at an application write-latency alarm if you have one. That would track what your users actually feel more closely.
   - FIS will not start an experiment while its stop-condition alarm is already in ALARM.

**Check the result**
7. Confirm the experiment has stopped. Expect `stopped`:
   `aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 --query 'experiment.state'`
8. Confirm the volume is back to its pre-incident baseline within about 3–5 minutes:
   - VolumeQueueLength about 0.8
   - about 1,000 IOPS
   - write latency about 1 ms/op
   - the alarm back to `OK`

   `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names example-d-gp3-queue-length --region us-east-1 --query 'MetricAlarms[0].StateValue'`

   `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Average --period 60 --start-time 2026-11-23T16:45:00Z --end-time <now> --region us-east-1`
9. Confirm the stop condition was saved:
   `aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --region us-east-1 --query 'experimentTemplate.stopConditions'`

**Rollback**
10. If the new stop condition gets in the way of the testing you intend, put back the original setting from the step 1 file:
    `aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --region us-east-1 --stop-conditions source=none`
11. If the owner wants the test back after it was stopped, start a new run:
    `aws fis start-experiment --experiment-template-id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --tags Project=example --region us-east-1`

### Risks and advisories
- Stopping the experiment ends a test someone deliberately started. The two earlier runs from this template (EXP1234567890abcdef_4 and EXP1234567890abcdef_8) were started and stopped by a person, so check with the owner before step 5.
- A stop condition on the volume's queue-length alarm will end the test as soon as it causes real queueing. If the test's purpose is to keep high latency going on purpose, use a higher threshold or an alarm on application impact instead.

### Durable prevention (configuration, for your infrastructure-as-code if the template is defined there)
- **Objective:** no FIS template that targets production-like EBS volumes should be able to run with `stopConditions: none`.
- **Acceptance criteria:**
  - `EXT1234567890abcdef_4` lists at least one `aws:cloudwatch:alarm` stop condition.
  - Running the template while that alarm is in ALARM stops the experiment.

### What I could not cover
- I did not find a repository or IaC source for this FIS template, so I give no repository location.
- I could not reach the template owner, so the decision to stop is still yours.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Write latency ~504 ms and queue length 16 on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** Average write latency on vol-0123456789abcdef0 (/dev/sdf on i-1234567890abcdef0_2) went from 0.953 ms to 503.6 ms. VolumeQueueLength went from ~0.77 to 16.0. IOPS fell from ~1,000 to 41.9 and throughput from 15.6 to 0.65 MiB/s. The queue-length alarm was expected to go into ALARM around 16:50–16:51Z.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T16:47:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 injects 500 ms I/O latency into vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** The aws:ebs:volume-io-latency action (500 ms on 100% of writes and 50% of reads, PT60M, started 16:47:16Z) explains the symptom exactly. Average write latency went from 0.95 ms to 503.6 ms at 16:48Z, and queue length rose to 16. The workload was steady at ~1,000 IOPS against 3,000 provisioned before onset. Instance EBS balance stayed at 99%, the other volumes were unaffected, and there were no Health events. The experiment was started manually with no stop condition, so it will run until about 17:47Z unless someone stops it.
**Cascades to:** symptom-vol-write-latency

#### Supporting Observations
- **Running FIS experiment injects I/O latency into vol-0123456789abcdef0:** FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (template EXT1234567890abcdef_4, role example-fis) has been running since 16:47:04Z. Its only target is vol-0123456789abcdef0. Its action is aws:ebs:volume-io-latency, started 16:47:16Z for PT60M: 500 ms latency on 100% of writes and 50% of reads. It has no stop conditions. The same template ran earlier today at 07:40 (completed), 08:35 and 16:15 (both stopped by a user).
- **Write latency jumped from 0.95 ms to ~504 ms at 16:47–16:48Z:** On vol-0123456789abcdef0, VolumeAvgWriteLatency held at a steady ~0.953 ms from 16:21 to 16:46Z. It rose to 3.8 ms at 16:47 and to 503.6 ms at 16:48Z, matching the injected 500 ms. VolumeQueueLength went from ~0.77 to 2.7 and then 16.0. Volume IOPS fell from a steady ~1,000 (about 500 writes and 500 reads per second, against 3,000 provisioned) to ~42, and throughput fell from 15.6 to 0.65 MiB/s. Idle time dropped from ~31 s to 0.46 s per minute. VolumeStalledIOCheck stayed at 0. The onset lines up with the FIS action start at 16:47:16Z. Before onset the workload was flat and far below its IOPS and throughput limits, so the volume was not saturated.
- **Instance EBS burst balance at 99%; CPU idle; other volumes unaffected:** On i-1234567890abcdef0_2 (c6i.large), EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% held at 99% minimum from 16:20 to 16:45Z, and CPU stayed around 1.4%. The instance-level EBS bottleneck is ruled out. Spare volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 had 0 write ops. Root volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_28 kept a normal ~45–117 writes per minute, so the degradation is limited to vol-0123456789abcdef0.
- **StartExperiment called manually by Admin/example-session at 16:47:04Z:** CloudTrail shows StartExperiment for template EXT1234567890abcdef_4 at 2026-11-23T16:47:04Z. The caller was [redacted ARN], using aws-cli from a Kiro IDE session (source IP 67.185.222.142, no MFA). It created EXP1234567890abcdef_7 with role example-fis, tags Project=example, and stopConditions source=none. The template, described as "example scenario d: 500 ms EBS I/O latency", was last updated at 16:47:01Z, three seconds before the start. After that, CloudTrail shows only read-only monitoring calls (GetExperiment and GetExperimentTemplate). No one has stopped the experiment.
- **Queue-length alarm fired in step with each past FIS run:** The example-d-gp3-queue-length alarm (VolumeQueueLength > 4, 3 of 3 one-minute datapoints, no actions) has fired in step with every past run of FIS template EXT1234567890abcdef_4: on 11-11 at 01:11 and 15:33, and on 11-23 at 07:43 and 08:39. When last checked it was still OK, last updated at 08:47:48Z. It had not yet crossed the threshold for 3 straight datapoints in the current run, which began at 16:47Z. It has no alarm actions, so no one gets notified.

#### Gaps
- **Only ~2 minutes of post-onset data:** Only about two minutes of metrics existed after the latency started at 16:47Z, so recovery and steady-state behaviour during the experiment were not seen.
- **Application metrics and logs not examined:** No application-level metrics or logs were examined. The application impact is inferred from EBS metrics only.

### Root Cause: Manually started FIS latency experiment with no stop condition
**Description:** Admin/example-session manually started FIS template EXT1234567890abcdef_4 ("example scenario d") at 16:47:04Z with aws-cli. The template targets only vol-0123456789abcdef0 and has no stop condition (source=none). The resulting experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 therefore injects 500 ms of I/O latency for the full 60 minutes, until about 17:47Z, unless someone stops it. Capacity is not the issue: IOPS and throughput sat at about 33% and 12.5% of provisioned, and there are no AWS-side faults. Adding IOPS would not help.
**Cascades to:** finding-fis-latency-injection

- **Write latency jumped from 0.95 ms to ~504 ms at 16:47–16:48Z:** On vol-0123456789abcdef0, VolumeAvgWriteLatency held at a steady ~0.953 ms from 16:21 to 16:46Z. It rose to 3.8 ms at 16:47 and to 503.6 ms at 16:48Z, matching the injected 500 ms. VolumeQueueLength went from ~0.77 to 2.7 and then 16.0. The instance-level EBS bottleneck is ruled out. Spare volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_16 had 0 write ops. Root volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_28 kept a normal ~45–117 writes per minute, so the degradation is limited to vol-0123456789abcdef0.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Stop FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (only after owner confirms the impact is unintended) and add an alarm-based stop condition to template EXT1234567890abcdef_4. Do not add IOPS.

## Reasoning
Latency is injected by FIS, not caused by saturation: the volume used ~33% of its 3,000 IOPS and 12.5% of 125 MiB/s before the test. Stopping the experiment returns the volume to its pre-experiment state; otherwise it ends on its own at ~17:47Z. The template has no stop condition, so future runs cannot halt themselves. The policy check's 'delete/terminate denied' flag on StopExperiment was judged a false positive: no resource or data is deleted.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Save the template as the rollback baseline
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --region us-east-1 > fis-template-EXT1234567890abcdef_4-before.json
```
**Purpose:** Save the template as the rollback baseline

#### 1.2 Save the experiment config so the test can be repeated exactly
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 > fis-experiment-EXP1234567890abcdef_7.json
```
**Purpose:** Save the experiment config so the test can be repeated exactly

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Confirm it is still running and only targets vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 --query 'experiment.{status:state.status,targets:targets.Volumes.resourceArns}'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm it is still running and only targets vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Advisory:** If the status is completed or stopped, skip stopping the experiment.

#### 2.2 Get the owner's go-ahead before stopping
**Type:** text
Get explicit confirmation from dewavic (Project=example) that the impact is unintended or unacceptable. If this is a planned test, let it finish at ~17:47Z.
**Purpose:** Get the owner's go-ahead before stopping

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 End the latency injection on the volume
**Type:** command
```
aws fis stop-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** End the latency injection on the volume
**Risks:** Ends a test someone deliberately started; a stopped experiment cannot be resumed, only re-run.

#### 3.2 Make future runs halt automatically on the queue-length alarm
**Type:** command
```
aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --region us-east-1 --stop-conditions source=aws:cloudwatch:alarm,value=[redacted ARN]
```
**Purpose:** Make future runs halt automatically on the queue-length alarm
**Advisory:** Does not affect the run already in progress., A queue-length stop condition ends the test as soon as it causes real queueing; use a higher threshold or an application-latency alarm if sustained latency is the goal., FIS will not start an experiment while its stop-condition alarm is already in ALARM.

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm the experiment shows stopped
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7 --region us-east-1 --query 'experiment.state'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the experiment shows stopped

#### 4.2 Confirm the volume returns to baseline within 3-5 min (queue ~0.8…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names example-d-gp3-queue-length --region us-east-1 --query 'MetricAlarms[0].StateValue'
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --statistics Average --period 60 --start-time 2026-11-23T16:45:00Z --end-time <now> --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the volume returns to baseline within 3-5 min (queue ~0.8, ~1,000 IOPS, ~1 ms writes, alarm OK)

#### 4.3 Confirm the stop condition was saved
**Type:** command
```
aws fis get-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --region us-east-1 --query 'experimentTemplate.stopConditions'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the stop condition was saved

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Remove the stop condition if it blocks intended testing
**Type:** command
```
aws fis update-experiment-template --id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --region us-east-1 --stop-conditions source=none
```
**Purpose:** Remove the stop condition if it blocks intended testing

#### 5.2 Start a new run if the owner wants the test back
**Type:** command
```
aws fis start-experiment --experiment-template-id EXT1234567890abcdef_4 --tags Project=example --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Start a new run if the owner wants the test back

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. No FIS template targeting production-like EBS volumes may run with stopConditions: none
**Description:** Codify an aws:cloudwatch:alarm stop condition on template EXT1234567890abcdef_4 in its IaC definition (no repository was found for it).
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- EXT1234567890abcdef_4 lists at least one aws:cloudwatch:alarm stop condition
- Running the template while that alarm is in ALARM stops the experiment

     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.

     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.

Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96

List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.

Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.

     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.

     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
